reason_for_upgrade: A deeper epigraphic and weapon-corpus pass recovered a highly distinctive Florence dagger, Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Firenze inv. 7677, whose published morphology and royal cartouche closely match the dagger shown on the Lima museum website. Until the image/object identity is resolved, the Lima website image must not be treated as proof that the photographed dagger is physically held in Lima.

inscription_gate.what_is_secure: The Lima museum and MINCETUR associate the visible marking with a pharaonic emblem/name, but no object-level specialist transliteration or translation for the Lima-held object has been recovered.

legacy_candidate.support: The Global Egyptian Museum legacy record classified Florence inv. 7677 under TUTHMOSIS III/MENKHEPERRE, and Menkheperre is securely the throne name of Thutmose III.

published_reassessment.interpretation: an otherwise unknown-looking variant close to Menkheperure, the coronation name of Thutmose IV
published_reassessment.note: The same article reports that the Global Egyptian Museum instead read Mn-kheper-Re-user and attributed the object to Thutmose III. The disagreement is itself evidence that the signs are not securely resolved from available photographs.

inscription_gate.working_plain_language: The inscription most likely contains a royal throne-name/cartouche in the Men-kheper-Re / Men-kheperu-Re family, but whether the intended king is Thutmose III or Thutmose IV remains open on current evidence.

chronology_control.rule: A circa-1200-BCE date does not by itself refute a Thutmose-III name.

evidence.finding: Late New Kingdom/Early Third Intermediate Period scarab ca. 1200-945 BCE contains the throne name Menkheperre and is interpreted as evidence of Thutmose III's posthumous cult.
Ramesside scarab ca. 1300-1080 BCE contains Menkheperre; the museum explicitly notes that Thutmose III's name continued to appear long after his reign.

chronology_control.implication: The Lima label '1200 AC' plus a Thutmose-III-associated name is chronologically possible in principle as posthumous/amuletic royal-name use; it cannot identify the manufacture date or king without object-level epigraphy and typology.

collection_provenance_gate.known_collection_mechanism: Miguel Mujica Gallo assembled Arms of the World through extensive foreign travel and active purchasing at auctions; public accounts also document international-auction acquisition activity.
